judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure all three OpenTelemetry signals with correct OTLP export
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are broadly workable and cover all signals, but B better matches the requested unified OTLP setup and supplies a cleaner minimal dependency set. A is weakened by repeated exporter configuration and its misleading appsettings example for environment-variable-style exporter settings.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Propagate trace context across a message queue
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers directly and correctly solve the propagation problem with usable publisher, consumer, and OpenTelemetry setup snippets. A has a small practical edge through its more tolerant header extraction and mention of null headers; B is otherwise comparably correct.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics with custom spans in ASP.NET Core
judgeRationales.rationale: Both largely provide workable OpenTelemetry tracing, OTLP export, a custom span, and a counter. B is preferable because it meets the important IMeterFactory dependency-injection requirement and makes source-name matching especially clear. A is more focused and has a clean explicit endpoint configuration, but its static Meter misses an explicit rubric requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Blazor Server app with CascadingAuthenticationState
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required .NET 8 Blazor Web App authentication and render-mode pattern: service-based cascading authentication, a separate interactive Routes component, antiforgery ordering, and explicit interactive server rendering. A performs much of the hosting conversion but misses the authentication-service requirement and does not activate interactivity.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add a new API endpoint to an existing controller-based project
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the basic controller-oriented shape and timestamp requirement, but B meets the key API-quality requirements around cancellation, sealed-record DTO design/naming, and XML documentation, while also adding validation and endpoint test coverage. A is a functional but substantially less aligned implementation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add error handling with ProblemDetails and IExceptionHandler
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are solid modern global-handling solutions with correct exception mappings and safe 500 behavior. B is modestly more complete for the broad requirement that all error responses use Problem Details because it also wires status-code pages, and it explicitly uses a sealed handler.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create a CRUD Web API with minimal APIs, OpenAPI, and proper HTTP semantics
judgeRationales.rationale: Both builds satisfy the basic API/service/OpenAPI task, but B aligns directly with the requested modern .NET API-quality rubric: Minimal APIs, typed result unions, sealed record DTOs, cancellation propagation, DateTimeOffset, and endpoint metadata chaining. A is a competent controller-based implementation but misses several explicit criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement secure file upload in ASP.NET Core 8 minimal API
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every stated security and implementation requirement, notably actual image signature validation. A has the core endpoint and limits but misses the explicit actual-content verification requirement, leaving type checks readily spoofable. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stream very large file uploads without buffering
judgeRationales.rationale: B is an actionable, largely correct implementation of streaming multipart uploads, including validation and safe file naming. A offers useful high-level statements but omits the essential code it promises, so it does not actually show how to implement the requested upload.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Upload multiple files with metadata in minimal API
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly matches the minimal-API form-binding use case and adds stronger content validation. Its WebP signature check is incomplete and the omitted MVC namespace may need adding in projects without an applicable using, but these do not outweigh the clearer [FromForm] solution. A remains a valid alternative via manual form parsing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure all three OpenTelemetry signals with correct OTLP export
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B better satisfies the core intent of the rubric: it uses a unified OTLP exporter (UseOtlpExporter) and keeps logging within the same AddOpenTelemetry builder so logs share the same resource/service identity as traces and metrics. Response A repeats the exporter config per signal and, importantly, configures logs via a separate pipeline that lacks the ConfigureResource call, meaning logs would not carry the service identity — failing rubric criteria 2 and 3. A is slightly more complete on package listing, but B wins the two most important criteria. Overall B is better, though A's response is also functional and correct in most respects, so the gap is moderate rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Propagate trace context across a message queue
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct, complete, and well-structured, covering inject, extract, and parent linkage properly. B is slightly better because it explicitly creates a Producer activity before injecting (the recommended messaging pattern), uses ActivityKind.Producer/Consumer on both sides, registers the custom ActivitySource in both services, and gives clear ordering guidance. A's injection uses Activity.Current without creating a dedicated producer span, and its extract carrier returns a single string rather than the array the propagator expects (a minor correctness concern), though it adds useful notes on W3C format and avoiding duplicate spans.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics with custom spans in ASP.NET Core
judgeRationales.rationale: B wins on the more technically significant criteria: using IMeterFactory via DI (modern best practice), configuring an appropriate resource service name, and explicitly noting name-matching requirements. A's advantage is staying focused without gratuitous logging/extra instrumentation, which B added unnecessarily. On balance, B satisfies more of the rubric's substantive correctness criteria, giving it a slight overall edge despite including extra unrequested features.

A failed on three key criteria — it kept the old CascadingAuthenticationState wrapper, never added the service, and omitted UseAntiforgery. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add a new API endpoint to an existing controller-based project
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agents faced an empty workspace lacking the referenced project. Response A pragmatically created a self-contained controller-based Orders API (GET/POST, OrderStatus enum, DTOs, in-memory service, DI wiring) and verified it builds, recovering from patch/encoding errors methodically. This is what the user actually wanted. Response B simply refused and asked for files, delivering no value—an overly conservative outcome given the task could be reasonably fulfilled with a self-contained implementation. While A doesn't clearly satisfy several of the finer rubric details (CancellationToken, CreatedAtAction, DateTimeOffset, XML docs) in its visible output, it addresses the core requirement and produced working code, whereas B produced nothing. A is much better overall."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Add error handling with ProblemDetails and IExceptionHandler
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide correct, modern IExceptionHandler implementations. B is better on several rubric points: it places the handler in a Middleware/ folder, uses generic detail messages avoiding leaking exception.Message, and adds UseStatusCodePages. A leaks exception.Message in Detail for known exceptions, which slightly weakens the no-sensitive-details goal. Overall B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Create a CRUD Web API with minimal APIs, OpenAPI, and proper HTTP semantics
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses produced working, tested .NET 10 Product APIs with correct 201/Location, enum-as-string serialization, and interface-backed services. However, the rubric strongly favors minimal APIs. Response A chose controllers (--use-controllers), which structurally fails criteria 1, 3, and 12 (TypedResults/Results<T> and .WithName/.WithSummary/.WithDescription are minimal-API idioms). Response B used the empty template with minimal APIs, aligning with the rubric's intent, and additionally set up XML documentation. Both were methodical and error-free, but B satisfies more rubric criteria on the specific API style demanded, making it meaningfully better."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement secure file upload in ASP.NET Core 8 minimal API
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high quality, satisfy all four rubric criteria, and are nearly identical in structure. B is slightly stronger on content validation: it uses a proper read loop to fully fill the magic-byte buffer (avoiding potential under-read of a single ReadAsync) and cross-checks declared vs detected content type. A adds ArrayPool micro-optimizations but its single ReadAsync could under-read the header. The difference is marginal, so B is only slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stream very large file uploads without buffering
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Upload multiple files with metadata in minimal API
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B satisfies all three rubric criteria fully: it sets both the Kestrel and FormOptions size limits, uses [FromForm] binding correctly, and stores files under GUID names. It also adds content-type and magic-byte validation. Response A only ties on filename handling; it fails to configure the multipart body length limit and doesn't demonstrate [FromForm] binding, relying on a less reliable RequestSizeLimitAttribute. Both are otherwise functional, but B is clearly stronger against the rubric."}
